finding: THE ENGINE'S RESULT HAS NO DURABLE HOME — persistence is the framework's most load-bearing prompt-only step, and it failed on the first wave that produced overturns.

finding: Cost claims were being estimated rather than measured, and three in one day were all wrong — each pointing at building the wrong thing.

finding: Plan mode had no slot for the owner's constraints, so at plan time the ticket got a voice and he did not.

finding: The run manifest measures PLUMBING, not YIELD — every health field can read green while almost nothing was buildable.
evidence: wf_33541300-121: misroutedLanes 0, waveFilesNamed 1, priorCleanDropped 0, log cutoff matched the watermark exactly — while 1 of 4 findings was ever dispatchable. Owner: 'Nothing build. But have open? And have reports. Where is our clean process.'

finding: A verify-raised dependency ask is deferred correctly and then scheduled NOWHERE.
evidence: A8 gave verify-raised FINDINGS a home (the discoveries array). Dependency asks got the same deferral rule and no destination. On wf_33541300-121 the verify flipped 158 to needs-dependency with a one-clause ask to instructor, and the run ended naming an incomplete fix with nothing scheduled to finish it.

finding: Agent definitions are session-cached too — the third loader, which completes the set. Engines (A9), skills (A13) and agent definitions all load once per session and none announces it.

Check with spend.cjs --day. Fix is a RULE, not code: a framework edit takes effect in a NEW session, and whoever makes one must say so.

finding: report.md's summary line is written by hand, not derived from the rows, so it can contradict the table directly beneath it
evidence: report.md:3 says '14 findings, 4 atomic, ZERO built' and 'Seven rows await you' while the table at :7 shows four rows marked built and six rows total

finding: node --check is a silent no-op on both engines, so every syntax verification of bugger.js and feature.js today reported success without parsing anything
evidence: Node v20.20.2 detects ESM syntax in a .js file and exits 0 WITHOUT parsing: identical bytes carrying a deliberate 'const x = {,}' exit 0 as .js and exit 1 as .mjs. .mjs is not the fix either — the engines use top-level return, illegal in a real module. Proven with a must-fail canary by the architect apply run; scripts/ledger-stats.cjs is .cjs so its check was real.

finding: bugger.js has no build mode, so the owner's rulings on a report can only leave the loop as hand dispatches
evidence: bugger.js:139 - MODE is collect or full and nothing else. feature.js already takes mode:build with pieces plus answers. On 2026-07-29 the owner ruled on report rows 160-166 across three messages and every ruling became a hand dispatch in session 995ebddb at 21:54 matchmaker, 22:13 instructor, 22:17 verifier, 22:49 matchmaker, 23:11 verifier, 23:38 matchmaker.
note: WHAT WE TRIED: nothing yet - this is the first time the asymmetry was named. WHAT WE LEARNED: the engine was NOT idle yesterday. wf_33541300-121 produced 36 ledger rows over 25 refs across 9 lanes, the largest engine contribution of any run in the window, and 2026-07-29 had the LOWEST hand-dispatch ratio of the four days measured (37 percent, against 94 on 07-26, 87 on 07-27, 64 on 07-28). So the defect is not that the engine builds too little. It is that the engine runs ONCE and then has no way back in. After it returns, the owner's decisions have no engine to receive them, so the second half of every bug wave runs with no funnel, no counts, no manifest and no inFlight tracking - which is exactly the half he said he could not follow. WHY THIS SOLUTION: feature.js solved this problem already with a two-phase plan-then-build shape, so this is not a new mechanism, it is deleting an inconsistency between two engines. The build loop at bugger.js:594 is reused verbatim; only the entry point is new. OBSERVABLE: the run manifest for a build-mode invocation names the approved refs it received and the count it dispatched, so a ruling the owner made that never reached a lane shows up as a number instead of as silence. RISK: a build-mode run that skips the scout also skips the openKnown and alreadyBuilt drops, so a stale approved ref could be rebuilt - the mode must still read the ledger.

finding: a verify DISCOVERY lands in the owner's live decide queue instead of the next run's intake, so a bonus finding gates the wave
evidence: In wf_33541300-121, 25 of 36 ledger rows carry source verify against 8 from github and 3 from both. Four rows say the literal words DISCOVERY, not built - availability-asserted-from-unsearched-window, classifier-guess-reaches-real-calendar-invite, nondirectory-email-accepted-and-defaulted, owner-shared-surface-set-never-read - and ledger-stats --open lists all four as DECIDE. Report rows 168-171 were discoveries and the owner was asked to rule on them at 23:37.
note: OWNER'S FRAMING, and it is the correct one: if i do want to fix discoveries, its not blocker, its bonus. WHAT WE LEARNED: the LABEL already exists and is written faithfully by the lanes; only the ROUTING is missing, so this is cheap. The verify produces two genuinely different things and the engine treats them identically. An OVERTURN says this wave's own work is wrong - gh#157-withheld-calendar-reported-as-absence and candidate-slots-branch-never-surfaced-unresolved-address both went built then overturned then built again - and an overturn MUST block, because shipping over it means shipping a known defect. A DISCOVERY is pre-existing ground the verify walked past, and it must NOT block, because the wave that found it did not cause it and cannot be held for it. WHY THIS SOLUTION: routing discoveries to the next run's intake removes 8 of yesterday's 25 refs from the decision the owner was trying to close, with nothing lost - they arrive as scout input on the following run, already shaped, and he can still promote one by naming it. It also stops the compounding case: three verify passes ran on one wave (one engine plus two hand at 22:17 and 23:11) and each added rows to a queue that was already open. WHY IT IS URGENT: prior runs produced 1 to 12 refs each; this one produced 25, and the verify is where the extra came from. OBSERVABLE: the report's decide section contains zero rows whose verdict text begins DISCOVERY, and the next run's scout brief names them as carried-in intake. RISK: a discovery that is actually severe - classifier-guess-reaches-real-calendar-invite can put an uninvited person on a real invite - must not be softened by being reclassified as a bonus. Severity and blocking are different axes, so the intake route needs to preserve severity. CORRECTED 2026-07-30, and the correction changes the work. This row's premise - that the label exists and only the ROUTING is missing - is WRONG. A8 (verdict built, 2026-07-27) already shipped the discoveries array and it is live in both engines: bugger.js:307 schema, :805 collect, :807 log, :899 and :981 and :1041 manifest and return, the same shape in feature.js. The mechanism is neither missing nor broken. What is wrong is the POLICY built on top of it: SKILL.md:227 says discoveries are next run's first item, never built in this wave, and then instructs Render discoveries as new rows at pending owner - so never-built-this-wave was implemented as still-on-his-desk-now, which is exactly the distinction the owner drew (not a blocker, a bonus). SKILL.md:372 then makes it mandatory by counting discoveries in persist.mustAlsoAppear. So the change lands in SKILL.md:227, SKILL.md:372 and the mustAlsoAppear counter, NOT in engine code, and this row AMENDS A8 rather than replacing it. TWO mechanisms failed to catch the overlap: the architect read its own ledger in review mode and still verified this as a missing mechanism, and architect-file.cjs:120 excludes built rows from its clash check so the filer never warned.

finding: nothing caps how many refs one run may put on the owner's desk, and the count doubled past every prior run without any signal
evidence: Refs per engine run across the window, from the ledger: wf_6b869440-ef7 4, wf_40d78c7e-80b 3, wf_b81e5b49-35b 8, wf_a9bc2bf7-43b 1, wf_a3bfe2a3-abe 4, wf_bb6eac4f-e8f 12, wf_33541300-121 25. capBuilds was 100. The manifest reported no ref count and no comparison to any prior run.
note: THIS IS THE ANSWER TO THE OWNER'S BEST QUESTION - its not our first bug run and every time I had comments, so why it worked then. It worked before because a run put 3 to 8 items on his desk. Yesterday it put 25, which is twice the previous maximum and six times the typical bug run. His pushback RATE was not unusual; the number of items each pushback had to be spent on was. WHAT WE LEARNED: the framework has a cap on BUILDS (capBuilds) and none on DECISIONS, yet decisions are the scarce resource - they are the only step that cannot be parallelised, batched or delegated, because there is one owner. A run that dispatches 100 fixes and asks him nothing is cheap; a run that dispatches 8 and asks him 25 questions is unfollowable, and the engine currently cannot tell those two apart. WHY THIS SOLUTION: a decision budget rather than a build budget. The engine already knows the number - it assembles the report - so this is a count and a warning, not a new mechanism, and it composes with A30: routing discoveries to intake is what brings 25 back under the budget without dropping anything. WHY NOT JUST A CAP: silently truncating to the first N would be the no-silent-caps failure. It must report what it held back and why. OBSERVABLE: the manifest prints refs-on-his-desk against the trailing average, and says so out loud when a run exceeds it - so the shape of yesterday would have been visible at 17:20 instead of at 23:50. RISK: a budget invites gaming by merging unrelated rows into one to stay under it, which is worse than 25 honest rows. The budget must trigger a warning and a deferral proposal, never a merge.

finding: the scout brief makes a ticket's TITLE the symptom and demotes its body to evidence, so a ticket listing three complaints yields one issue
evidence: bugger.js:467 - the ref is #<number> and the symptom is the title; the evidence is the body plus any file:line it names. gh#156 body carries three numbered complaints and the scout returned one issue (flow-narrates-unexecuted-actions). gh#158 carries three and the scout returned one (158-attendee-misresolution). Neither was a drop: droppedAsOpenKnown was gh#155 and gh#154 only, droppedAsAlreadyBuilt was empty.
note: WHAT WE LEARNED: the owner writes tickets as a pasted Slack transcript followed by a numbered list of what went wrong - gh#156 ends with 1. why first going to online or person 2. why she lied 3. what does getting back to you mean. That numbered list IS the work. The brief instructs the scout to treat the title as the symptom, so the list becomes supporting evidence for a single title-shaped issue, and two of the three complaints were never surfaced by any run. They reached report.md as rows 173 and 174 only at 00:18 when the OWNER named them himself, and report.md records the consequence in its own words: gh#156's other two complaints, which no scout has ever surfaced. WHY THIS SOLUTION: one line of the brief, inverted - enumerate the complaints in the body FIRST and emit one issue per complaint, then use the title only as a label for the group. The atomic-split rule the scout charter already holds then does the rest. WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND gh#156: this is also why every ticket ended PARTIAL and nothing could close. Three tickets went in, each with three complaints, and the run engaged with one complaint per ticket. OBSERVABLE: the scout reports complaintsFound per ticket against issuesEmitted, so 3-in-1-out is visible in the manifest rather than invisible until the owner reads the ticket himself. RISK: a body with a long transcript and no numbered list has no complaints to enumerate, and forcing a count there would invent issues. The rule must be enumerate what is explicitly listed, never infer a list that is not there.

finding: when the scout merges a GitHub ticket with a log moment the merged row loses the ticket number, so ticket coverage cannot be computed for it
evidence: In wf_33541300-121 the two single-source rows kept their parent - 158-attendee-misresolution and 157-calendar-filter-and-history-gap - while the one row with source both became flow-narrates-unexecuted-actions with no 156 anywhere in it. gh#158 therefore got an explicit coverage row reading TICKET COVERAGE: partial - do NOT close #158 on this wave, and gh#156 got none, because no ref in the run named it.
note: WHAT WE LEARNED: this is the more dangerous half of the scout problem, because it is silent in a way A32 is not. A32 loses complaints; this loses the LINK, and once the link is gone nothing downstream can notice anything is missing. The coverage check is not broken - it worked perfectly for gh#158 - it simply had no row to fire on for gh#156. That is the framework's signature failure shape once more: a mechanism that does nothing and looks exactly like success, because a ticket with no coverage row is indistinguishable from a ticket with nothing wrong. WHY THIS SOLUTION: make the parent ref structural rather than conventional. A merged row keeps the ticket ref and gains the log evidence, so source both means both sources are named, not that the weaker id wins. This is also the same fix the owner proposed independently for dependency numbering - see the sibling row on report ids - and the two should be built as one change, because both are the rule that every id derives from its parent. WHY IT IS CHEAP: the ledger ALREADY does parent-scoped refs correctly (gh#158-exception-must-be-name-scoped), so the convention exists and is proven; only the merge path departs from it. OBSERVABLE: every ticket named in the scout's input appears in at least one ref in the run's output, and the manifest lists any ticket that does not. Run against yesterday, gh#156 appears. RISK: forcing a parent onto a genuinely source-less log finding would create fake ticket links. The rule applies only where a ticket was actually merged in.

finding: report row ids are a flat counter, so a blocker raised on a ticket gets an unrelated number and the ids collide with GitHub issue numbers
evidence: state.json nextReportId is 175 and yesterday's rows were 160-174, while the ledger refs for the same work are parent-scoped (gh#158-exception-must-be-name-scoped). Report rows 164 and 165 existed at the same time as gh#164 and gh#165, filed 2026-07-29 at 18:24 and 18:30, and the owner rules by bare number - 165 - lets ignore it.
note: OWNER'S DESIGN, in his words: if you had ticket 153 and you got something that block it, it won't be 170, it will be 153-blockA or something. WHAT WE LEARNED: there are two id systems and they disagree. The ledger already uses parent-scoped refs and gets this right; the REPORT uses a flat counter, and the report is the surface he actually reads and rules on. So the good convention exists in the place nobody looks and the bad one is in the place where decisions are made. Three separate problems collapse into this one change. First, a raised blocker becomes traceable at a glance - 153-blockA says what it blocks, 170 says nothing. Second, coverage becomes arithmetic rather than prose: a ticket with three complaints that emitted 156-a only is VISIBLY incomplete without anyone writing a coverage sentence, which is what failed for gh#156. Third, the collision with GitHub numbers disappears, because 156-a can never be mistaken for an issue number while 165 always can. WHY THIS SOLUTION AND NOT A PREFIX: a prefix like R165 would fix only the collision and would leave the parent unnamed, so it solves the smallest of the three. WHY IT IS SAFE: the counter's own rule - never renumber, never reuse - is preserved by keeping the flat sequence for rows with no parent, and only rows derived from a ticket or from another row take the derived form. OBSERVABLE: no report row id is a bare integer that also exists as an open GitHub issue number, and every child row's id contains its parent's. RISK: state.json's nextReportId note says ids must be stable forever because 14 must mean the same thing next month. Migrating existing rows would break that, so this applies to NEW rows only and the flat ones keep their numbers.

finding: report.md says nothing is waiting on you at the wrap while 48 rows are open, 9 of them raised by the run that just wrapped
evidence: report.md:3 reads Empty - v4.3.2 wrapped. Nothing is waiting on you. At the same commit ledger-stats --open returns 49 rows awaiting him. wf_33541300-121 alone left 15 unresolved refs (11 open plus 4 deferred) and the report carries 6 of them, so about 9 are ledger-only - including classifier-guess-reaches-real-calendar-invite at createMeeting.ts:150-156, which can put a person the owner never named onto a real invite.
note: OWNER'S WORDS: i also didn't understand how the report is empty and i have 49 items. WHAT WE LEARNED: this is the framework's signature failure standing on the owner-facing surface at the single moment he trusts it most - the wrap. The wrap protocol empties report.md because the wave is finished, and finished is being read as nothing is owed. Those are different claims. The rows did not go anywhere; they moved to a file with no headline, so the surface that says nothing is waiting is the one surface that never counts. HIS SECOND POINT, and it is the fix: add report sections by STATUS - deferred, open, declined - instead of one undifferentiated decide list, so the open set is always visible and always counted. HIS THIRD POINT, which needs checking before building: maybe many of them are not relevant. Measured, the 48 open rows last moved on 07-26 (4), 07-27 (7), 07-28 (7) and 07-29 (30), so about 18 rows are two to four days stale and several describe code that later waves have changed. So the report cannot simply print all 48 - a stale row is worse than a missing one, exactly as the verifiedClean list already warns. The status sections need an age column and a rule for retiring a row whose code has moved. WHY THIS SOLUTION: the count already exists in ledger-stats. The report does not need to hold the rows, only to state the true number and where to see them, so at minimum the wrap must never print a zero it did not compute. OBSERVABLE: the number in report.md's headline equals the number ledger-stats --open returns, checkable in one command at any moment. RISK: printing 48 rows every time trains him to ignore the section, which is how the report got emptied in the first place.

finding: a finished run wakes the chat and the chat stays silent, so a completed wave can sit unread for hours
evidence: In session 995ebddb the task-notification for wf_33541300-121 arrived at 17:20 local on 2026-07-29 and the next event in the transcript is the owner at 21:32 saying show me the report - 4h12m of a finished run sitting unread. He filed gh#164 and gh#165 at 18:24 and 18:30, inside that gap. A PushNotification tool is present in the harness and grep for its tool_use in that session returns 0.
note: OWNER'S QUESTION: how they can tell me, i can read chat. ANSWER, and it corrects the natural assumption: the notification is NOT missing. The harness woke the chat at 17:20 with the run's result in hand. What is missing is that the Manager wrote the report and then stopped, because nothing in the protocol says a returned run must reach him rather than merely be recorded. So the loop is silent by design, not by accident. WHAT WE LEARNED: this is the cheapest fix in the whole set and it changes the shape of the day more than any of them. Yesterday's decision phase started at 21:32 and ran to 00:31 - past midnight, which is why the last four decisions were move to tomorrow, already late. Those deferrals are not judgement, they are the clock, and the clock was set by a four-hour gap that nobody was told about. Had he seen the report at 17:20 the same 25 refs would have had five working hours instead of three night ones. It also caused the id collision: gh#164 and gh#165 were filed during the gap because he had no reason to think a wave was waiting. WHY THIS SOLUTION: one PushNotification call in the Manager's post-run protocol, carrying the count that matters - refs on his desk, tickets touched, whether a verify is still owed. Not a new mechanism; a tool that already exists and has never once been called. OBSERVABLE: the gap between a run's return timestamp and his first turn on it, which is measurable from any transcript and was 252 minutes yesterday. RISK: a push per lane return would be noise. It fires on a RUN returning and on nothing else.

The defect is not the decision, it is that the decision was invisible at the moment it mattered. The wrap is the last gate before real people see the change, and it summarised six product fixes without distinguishing the four that a verifier had adversarially read from the two that only their own author had. finding: the open backlog has no retirement path, so a finding whose code has since moved stays open forever and inflates the count

The open list has the mirror-image failure and no rule: a stale open row does not silence anything, it DILUTES - it makes 48 look like 48 real decisions when some number of them describe code that no longer exists, and that is what makes the whole list unreadable and therefore unread. The architect's own ledger has the identical disease - 17 open rows, oldest last touched 07-26, no pruning rule and no re-read stamp - so the retirement path lands once in ledger-stats and serves the bug ledger and the architect ledger together. finding: the tier-consistency check in spend.cjs passes for an agent whose every run contradicts its charter, because it compares engine rows against hand rows rather than against the charter file
evidence: spend.cjs --day 2026-07-29 prints: Tier is consistent for all 10 chartered agents - no dispatch path is overriding the charter. At that same moment .claude/agents/architect.md declared model: sonnet, and all three architect runs that day were opus (130, 97 and 52 turns). The architect has only ever been hand-dispatched, so it owns no engine row to disagree with and the check passes on a set of one.
note: WHAT WE LEARNED: this is the framework's signature failure living inside the tool built to measure the framework - a check that reads green while the thing it checks is false. The wording is what makes it dangerous: no dispatch path is overriding the charter is a claim about the CHARTER, and the code only ever compares two dispatch paths to each other. For any agent dispatched by exactly one path - which is every hand-only agent, and the architect is one - the comparison has a single member, agrees with itself, and reports consistency it never tested. WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND THE ARCHITECT: the tier is the dominant cost lever in the whole loop (opus cache-read 1.50 against sonnet 0.30), and this is the only automated check on it. A silent pass here is how a lane could run a tier above its charter for a week at four to five times the cost with the report saying everything is fine. WHY THIS SOLUTION: read the model field out of the agent .md and compare observed tier against DECLARED tier, which is the comparison the sentence already promises. The charter files are right there and the fix is smaller than the check it replaces. OBSERVABLE: run it against 2026-07-29 with architect.md declaring sonnet and the line must report the architect as overriding; today, with the charter reading opus, the same data must report consistent. A check that cannot fail on known-bad input is not a check. RISK: an agent with no model field in its frontmatter inherits the session default, so absent must mean not-checked and be reported as such rather than silently counted as agreeing.

finding: the clash check in architect-file.cjs excludes built rows, so a row that re-raises an already-shipped mechanism is filed with no warning
